detail.abstract:
Abstracts. “The Constitutional Law-Making Process: Theory and Practice through the Constitutions of Vietnam” analyzes the formulation and implementation of Vietnam’s Constitutions across different historical periods. It compares the theoretical foundations of constitutional law with the country’s specific socio-political realities.

The article explores key questions, such as whether the Vietnamese Constitutions of 1946, 1959, 1980, 1992, and 2013 genuinely reflect and uphold universal constitutional principles or whether they primarily function as legal instruments serving the political agenda of the ruling Party.

It also addresses the practical respect for constitutional norms, particularly the tension between the Communist Party’s leadership role and constitutional supremacy. The article advocates for reforms to ensure the Constitution becomes a truly democratic document—capable of reshaping the relationship between the State, the Party, and the People in a more balanced and modern direction. One such reform includes the establishment of an independent Constitutional Court.

Overall, the article offers a critical and scholarly perspective on Vietnam’s constitutional evolution, highlighting its strengths, shortcomings, and the challenges ahead in building a robust legal foundation for the country’s future.

detail.abstract: This paper proposes the concept of the Bureaucracy-Dominated Centralized Power State Model to analyze the structure and governance of China's political system. The model emphasizes centralized decision-making, bureaucratic dominance in policy implementation, ideological unity, and limited citizen political participation. Through case studies and theoretical analysis, this paper explores the model's impact on policy efficiency, social stability, and democratic participation, and compares it with Western democracies and other authoritarian regimes. The aim is to provide a novel analytical tool for comparative political research.

title: On Fairness of Process Flexibility
affiliations: , National University of Singapore (NUS) and Shanghai Jiao Tong University (SJTU) - Antai College of Economics and Management

detail.title: On Fairness of Process Flexibility
detail.abstract: Many studies have supported that a sparse process flexibility structure can capture nearly all of the benefits of full flexibility in terms of demand satisfaction and capacity utilization. While the efficiency metrics have been well assessed in the literature, the performance of sparse structures with respect to fairness measures remains under-explored. Fairness is a crucial objective in many resource allocation scenarios, such as humanitarian logistics and healthcare operations. In this study, we investigate the worst-case performance of sparse flexibility structures in terms of the max-min demand fill rate and min-max demand shortfall. We show that the max-min fill rate of a structure is determined by the demand subset with the minimum ratio of neighboring capacity to demand. Building on this characterization, we characterize the worst-case max-min fill rate of k-chain and Ψ-expander structures. We further show that there exist allocation decisions that simultaneously achieve max-flow (efficiency) and the max-min fill rate (fairness); such solutions can be obtained via a linear program. Our results suggest that fairness performance depends critically on the worst-covered subset of demand nodes and higher connectivity is needed to design a "fair" flexibility structure. We validate our theoretical findings using real-world data from the Texas Department of State Health Services and conclude that incorporating flexibility structure design can substantially enhance both fairness and efficiency in vaccine allocation.

title: Digital Resistance: Electronic Literature as Counter-Market Practice

detail.title: Digital Resistance: Electronic Literature as Counter-Market Practice
detail.abstract: This study investigates the emergence of electronic literature as a counter-market practice within contemporary digital culture, examining how digital literary works establish resistant practices while operating within neoliberal market structures. The research demonstrates how digital literary innovation establishes new value paradigms that challenge market-driven literary production through critically analyzing electronic literary works. This research advances scholarly understanding of cultural production under digital capitalism by demonstrating how electronic literature establishes creative practices that maintain critical independence while acknowledging their embeddedness within broader economic structures. The paper presents new theoretical possibilities for conceptualizing literary value and political engagement within an increasingly platform-mediated cultural landscape.

title: Strategic Agility in Institutional Voids: How Ambidextrous Leadership Asymmetrically Deploys Exploration and Exploitation in High Power-Distance Emerging Markets
affiliations: Addis Ababa University

detail.title: Strategic Agility in Institutional Voids: How Ambidextrous Leadership Asymmetrically Deploys Exploration and Exploitation in High Power-Distance Emerging Markets
detail.abstract: Institutional voids and high power-distance (HPD) reshape the pursuit of strategic agility in emerging markets (EMs). Drawing on institutional theory and the dynamic capabilities perspective, we develop and test the Dynamic Leadership Synthesis (DLS) model, reconceptualizing ambidextrous leadership as asymmetrically deployed in HPD institutional voids.Using a three-wave, multi-source dataset of 581 leaders and 2,324 subordinates in Ethiopia’s banking sector—a paradigmatic case of rapid growth amid institutional fragility—we show that Leadership Competency (LC) drives business performance predominantly through the Exploitation Strategic Pathway (LC → Organizational Culture → Performance), which is 2.23× stronger than the Exploration Pathway (LC → Employee Engagement → Performance).Moreover, Transformational Leadership selectively amplifies the Exploration Pathway, supporting renewal, whereas Transactional Leadership fortifies the dominant Exploitation Pathway by embedding operational efficiency and legitimizing adaptive norms in hierarchical structures.These findings indicate that in institutional voids, strategic agility emerges not from balanced Exploration–Exploitation, but from leadership acting as a quasi-institutional mechanism, embedding stable Exploitation capacity into organizational culture. This study advances a globally inclusive theory of asymmetric ambidextrous leadership, challenges universalist assumptions, and provides actionable guidance for building performance in institutionally constrained EM contexts.

title: The Echo of Leadership – How Employee Perceptions of CEOs Permeate Organizational Boundaries and Influence Financial Outcomes
affiliations: Bentley University, Fordham University   and Fordham University - Gabelli School of Business

detail.title: The Echo of Leadership – How Employee Perceptions of CEOs Permeate Organizational Boundaries and Influence Financial Outcomes
detail.abstract: Drawing on management theories, including Ethical Leadership, Social Exchange Theory, and Leader–Member Exchange, this study examines whether employee perceptions of Chief Executive Officers (CEOs) influence external financing outcomes. Using over half a million Glassdoor reviews (2012–2018) merged with data on 46,623 corporate bonds issued by 853 U.S. firms, we investigate the association between CEO approval and firms’ cost of debt and credit ratings. We find that higher CEO approval predicts better credit ratings and lower at-issue bond yield spreads, with effects particularly strong for smaller, highly leveraged, and speculative-grade firms. These relationships remain robust after controlling for firm and CEO characteristics, addressing endogeneity through instrumental variables, investor attention tests, and change regressions. CEO approval also forecasts higher subsequent profitability and market valuation and mitigates the negative debt cost impact of the COVID-19 crisis. Our findings position employee voice as a strategic intangible asset with value relevance for capital markets, extending management theories into the domain of external stakeholder decision-making. This work contributes to the literature on leadership effectiveness, organizational signaling, and the financial implications of employee perceptions, highlighting the role of internal sentiment in shaping external financing conditions.

title: From Insight to Impact: Closing the Marketing Science Value Chain with Interactive, Research-Driven Apps
affiliations: , Alma Mater Studiorum University of Bologna, VU University Amsterdam and Independent

detail.title: From Insight to Impact: Closing the Marketing Science Value Chain with Interactive, Research-Driven Apps
detail.abstract: Every year, several thousands of marketing articles are published in academic journals, often with the aim of disseminating new insights not only to the academic community but also to managerial practice. However, there is wide acknowledgment of gaps in the marketing science value chain, hindering the flow of marketing knowledge to other researchers and managers. We posit that interactive, research-driven (IRD) apps that provide a deeper understanding of the usability of the research contribution are a viable solution to improve the diffusion of marketing knowledge. We shed light on the motivations and barriers to develop IRD apps as well as the market potential and impact of IRD apps through a multi-method examination, which includes interviews, secondary data analyses, and experimental studies. We find an untapped potential of IRD apps among published articles and complementary evidence of their value to researchers and managers. We further provide a tutorial to guide the development of IRD apps that complement static research papers, and close with a forward looking section about the future of IRD apps. We hope that our examination stimulates other researchers to complement their articles with IRD apps that enable the diffusion of research findings to other researchers and managers.

title: Ten Structural Shifts in AI Adoption: Evidence, Frameworks, and Emerging Frontiers (2018 -2025)

detail.title: Ten Structural Shifts in AI Adoption: Evidence, Frameworks, and Emerging Frontiers (2018 -2025)
detail.abstract: Recent developments in AI adoption within financial institutions between 2018 and 2025 are synthesized using three established frameworks: the FinTech Pyramid, T-Shaped Teams, and Adapted Bloom's Taxonomy. By interpreting academic research, industry surveys, and regulatory reports, this paper identifies ten major structural shifts marking the sector's progression from experiments to institutionalization. The findings reveal that AI is reorganizing finance through integrated changes in technology, organization, and culture, emphasizing the rising importance of leadership, values-driven AI governance, and human-machine collaboration in the era of rapid AI advancement.

title: An Automatic Synchronous Calibration Method for Non-contact 3D Reconstruction Based on Cross-structured Light
affiliations: Beijing Information Science and Technology University

detail.title: An Automatic Synchronous Calibration Method for Non-contact 3D Reconstruction Based on Cross-structured Light
detail.abstract: This paper proposes an automatic synchronous calibration method based on cross-structured light for non-contact 3D reconstruction, aiming to enhance automation, accuracy, and adaptability of industrial measurement. Unlike traditional line structured light systems which require manual movement of calibration targets and separate calibration of the camera and light plane, this method leverages the geometric invariance of the intersection points of crossed lasers to simultaneously solve for camera intrinsic parameters, extrinsic parameters, and light plane parameters in a single set of images, thereby integrating calibration and measurement.  Additionally, the system incorporates a dual-exposure fusion strategy and collaborates with a robotic arm to significantly improve dynamic range and reduce interference from highly reflective surfaces on measurements. Experimental results show that under standard industrial conditions, the calibration error of this system can be controlled within ±0.5 mm, with an average reconstruction accuracy of ±0.25 mm, and the peak error rate is below 2.67%. Compared with traditional methods, this system effectively improves the dynamic range of measurement. This method provides an efficient, low-cost, fully automated solution for industrial quality inspection, reverse engineering, and surface morphology analysis.

title: Toyota Studies: The Way Forward - Expecting Leadership from Everyone
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Toyota Studies: The Way Forward - Expecting Leadership from Everyone
detail.abstract: This paper illustrates that Toyota Motor Corporation's management system integrates TPDS+TPS+TSS+Deming's "system-based production" into a single, functioning whole. It further demonstrates that a generalized version of this management system replaces the GMderived management approach that persists to this day. This is a management system that systematically creates various intangible assets by investing intellectual capital and human capital. Intellectual assets encompass various deliverables, human capabilities, and organizational capabilities. The value of these intangible assets is evaluated in relation to PMF (Product Market Fit). Since the 1980s, Toyota's management system has been studied in Europe and America. Today, under names like Lean and Agile, what is considered the Toyota-style management system is being implemented worldwide. However, its application in actual business has not yielded the expected results. In 2016, while writing a book on the Toyota Management System, I met many researchers and gained an understanding of the current situation. This paper corrects major misconceptions from past research. It promotes the implementation of a revised Toyota Management System across all industries, including not only manufacturing companies but also healthcare and administrative services. Furthermore, this paper demonstrates that the Toyota Management System serves as the reference model for management in the new capitalist economic era, centered on intellectual capital and human capital. It shows that this system forms the foundation of the economics of this new capitalist era̶that is, the modern economics centered on intangibles.

title: The Effect of Platform-Developed AI Price Recommendations Adoption on E-Commerce Platform Sales Revenue Distribution
affiliations: National University of Singapore (NUS), National University of Singapore (NUS) and New York University (NYU) - Leonard N. Stern School of Business

detail.title: The Effect of Platform-Developed AI Price Recommendations Adoption on E-Commerce Platform Sales Revenue Distribution
detail.abstract: Past studies on the long-tail phenomenon in digital markets or platforms have yet examined how emerging platform-developed AI pricing agents affect the sales revenue distribution of products on ecommerce platforms (ECPs). To fill this gap, we use a proprietary dataset from a leading Asian ECP to empirically quantify the effect of sellers' adoption of platform-developed AI price recommendations on the sales revenue distribution of products. By using ordinary least squares (OLS) regression models at the seller-product and category levels with an instrumental variable (IV) identification approach, we consistently find that AI pricing adoption leads to a more diverse sales revenue distribution of products. Specifically, at the seller-product level, we find that AI pricing adoption enhances sales revenue for both high- and low-popularity products. However, AI pricing disproportionately benefits low-popularity products and fosters a more diverse sales revenue distribution, such that high-popularity products experience a 49.0% lower sales revenue increase compared to low-popularity ones. At the category level, a 10% increase in AI pricing adoption share is linked to a 0.014-unit reduction in the Gini coefficient of the category sales revenue. Furthermore, we find that this effect is stronger when market competition is more intense. At the seller-product level, the revenue-boosting effect of AI pricing for high-popularity products is attenuated by 0.63% when the number of competitors increases by 10%. At the category level, a 10% increase from the average number of products per category is associated with an additional 0.003-unit decrease in the Gini coefficient. Mechanism analyses reveal that AI pricing diversifies sales revenue distribution by increasing product visibility, conversion rate, and purchase quantity, all more salient for low-popularity products. Additional analysis shows that AI pricing adoption enables sellers to set more competitive, generally lower prices, and to respond more effectively to price competition. Overall, this study theoretically contributes to research on the effects of AI pricing on long-tail sales distribution, digital divide, and competition on ECPs, and provides pivotal practical implications to ECP operators, sellers, and regulators.

title: The Effect of Perceived Corporate Social Responsibility and Green Brand Positioning as Sustainability Branding Strategies on Customer Purchase Intention: A Study on Household Electronic Goods Industry

detail.title: The Effect of Perceived Corporate Social Responsibility and Green Brand Positioning as Sustainability Branding Strategies on Customer Purchase Intention: A Study on Household Electronic Goods Industry
detail.abstract: The present study intends to identify the effect of sustainable branding strategies on consumer purchase intention. Under sustainable branding strategies, the study identifies the effect of green brand positioning and perceived CSR on consumer purchase intention. The study has been conducted on consumers of household electronic appliances. The researcher applied regression analysis using SPSS for data analysis collecting the data from 322 respondents. The findings of the study show that green brand positioning has a significant influence on consumer purchase intention. Similarly, perceived CSR also has a substantial impact on consumer purchase intention. The present study is original and has made a noteworthy contribution as it identifies two significant predictors of consumer purchase intention. Future researchers may include more predictor variables to overcome the study's limitations.

title: Visual Identity as Strategic Signal: How Corporate Logos Encode Innovation Orientation
affiliations: and University of Iowa - Henry B. Tippie College of Business

detail.title: Visual Identity as Strategic Signal: How Corporate Logos Encode Innovation Orientation
detail.abstract: Existing logo research almost exclusively adopts a "consumer perspective" paradigm that treats logos as marketing stimuli and examines their effects, but neglects the supply side: Why do firms design logos this way? Do logos reflect firms' strategic orientations? We introduce a strategic signaling perspective on corporate logos, demonstrating that visual design systematically encodes firms' strategic orientations. Using computer vision and machine learning, we find that visual features predict R&D intensity and capital expenditure intensity significantly above chance. Innovation-intensive firms exhibit distinct visual language: lower complexity, higher symmetry, blue-dominant palettes, and greater white space. Encoding effectiveness varies by industry context, consistent with strategic heterogeneity theory. Critically, logo features predict both internal strategic metrics (R&D from financial statements) and external market perceptions (volatility from trading data), demonstrating convergent validity. This alignment suggests logos reflect genuine strategic orientations that consistently shape both visual identity choices and market performance. This research reconceptualizes logos from marketing stimuli to strategic signals, bridging branding and strategic management literatures. We provide a framework for logo auditing and demonstrate that visual identity decisions have implications beyond consumer marketing.

detail.abstract: We provide experimental evidence on how employers adjust expectations to automation risk in high-skill, white-collar work. Using a randomized information intervention among tax advisors in Germany, we show that firms systematically underestimate automatability. Information provision raises risk perceptions, especially for routine-intensive roles. Yet, it leaves short-run hiring plans unchanged. Instead, updated beliefs increase productivity and financial expectations with minor wage adjustments, implying within-firm inequality like limited rent-sharing. Employers also anticipate new tasks in legal tech, compliance, and AI interaction, and report higher training and adoption intentions.

title: The Korean Paradox: How A Nation Balances Glamour with Grind

detail.title: The Korean Paradox: How A Nation Balances Glamour with Grind

detail.abstract: South Korea is globally admired for its cultural influence and economic strength, but few recognize the paradox at the heart of its rise. This research explores what can be termed THE KOREAN PARADOX: the nation's ability to balance two seemingly opposite forces namely, glamour and grind, which has made it both a cultural trendsetter and an economic powerhouse. On the one hand, the global appeal of Korean soft power: K-pop, K-drama, K-beauty and cutting-edge design. On the other hand, the country's relentless work culture, competitive education system, and corporate discipline, have helped its rise from a war-torn nation to a global leader. Through the lens of business and culture, this study examines how South Korea has worked to develop a dual brand identity. It looks at the role of major conglomerates such as Samsung, Hyundai, LG and SK in building Korea's global credibility, and how pop culture reinforced national branding on an emotional level. Special focus is given to the Hyundai and BTS partnership, which represents the perfect fusion of Korea's industrial might and cultural resonance. From the perspective of business and management, the study treats this concept not merely as a cultural exploration but a strategic case study. It analyses how contrast, when intentionally managed can function as a national asset. The Korea model offers valuable insights for leaders and policymakers navigating the balance between performance and perception, tradition and innovation. This study does not seek to glorify or criticize South Korea. Rather, it presents a nuanced analysis of how a nation transforms its internal contradictions into a competitive advantage, offering a distinctive contribution to debates on national branding, soft power, and sustainable development.

detail.abstract: Utilizing the staggered legalization of sports gambling across states, we provide causal evidence of the impact of gambling on physical activity. title: Corporate Taxation and Firm Productivity

detail.title: Corporate Taxation and Firm Productivity
detail.abstract: This paper examines the relationship between corporate taxes and productivity using a global sample of over four million firms. Employing an unconditional quantile regression approach, we demonstrate that taxes affect firms differently along the distribution of productivity. Higher taxes force low-productivity firms out of the market, reallocating resources to more productive firms and raising productivity at the lower end of the distribution. However, higher taxes also reduce incentives for productivity-enhancing investments, negatively impacting firms at the upper end of the productivity distribution. Lastly, we find that higher corporate taxes lower the probability that firms move up within the productivity distribution over time. Our findings demonstrate that governments can use corporate tax policy to foster productivity growth, but highlight the importance of accounting for its heterogeneous effects.

title: Reproducible Admission Serum Bicarbonate Thresholds Distinct from Normal Range Predict In-Hospital Mortality in Critically Ill Patients: An International Study with Personalized Survival Curves

detail.title: Reproducible Admission Serum Bicarbonate Thresholds Distinct from Normal Range Predict In-Hospital Mortality in Critically Ill Patients: An International Study with Personalized Survival Curves

keywords.keywords: Serum bicarbonate; In-hospital mortality; Causal inference; Threshold; Causal SurvivalNet; Prediction model

detail.abstract:
Background: Bicarbonate abnormalities are common in ICU patients, yet prior mortality studies have focused on non-critical care populations, overlooking pathophysiology specific to critical illness. This large-scale international cohort study aimed to identify optimal admission serum bicarbonate thresholds for predicting mortality in ICU patients and develop a deep learning-based personalized survival prediction model. 

Methods: We analyzed admission data from 208,072 adult ICU patients from the US and China, including demographics, comorbidities, and laboratory/vital signs. The primary outcome was in-hospital mortality. Using fast causal inference, we first identified significant admission variables linked to mortality. To model the nonlinear relationship between serum bicarbonate and mortality, we developed an integrated statistical framework (combining restricted cubic splines with Cox and frailty models) to quantify risk and identify high-risk thresholds. Subsequently, we developed Causal SurvivalNet, an adaptive deep neural network, and launched a corresponding web-based tool for real-time risk stratification.  

Results: Admission serum bicarbonate was significantly associated with in-hospital mortality. Restricted cubic spline analysis identified crucial bicarbonate thresholds at 24 mEq/L and 33 mEq/L. Compared to the reference range of 24–33 mEq/L, patients with bicarbonate levels ≤24 mEq/L or >33 mEq/L had a significantly higher mortality risk (adjusted HR 1.22, 95% CI: 1.16 - 1.28 and HR 1.17, 95% CI: 1.02 - 1.35, respectively). These findings were consistent across the US and Chinese cohorts. The Causal SurvivalNet model accurately generated personalized survival curves, achieving strong performance with integrated Brier scores of 0.15, 0.076, and 0.16 at different time points. This clinical tool is accessible at https://bicarbonate.deepsurvival.cc/. 

Conclusion: We identified reproducible serum bicarbonate thresholds (≤24 and >33 mEq/L) at ICU admission that are causally associated with in-hospital mortality across international cohorts. Our novel deep learning model, incorporating these thresholds and other causal variables, achieved superior performance in personalized survival prediction compared to conventional approaches. These findings highlight the utility of admission bicarbonate levels for early risk stratification and individualized outcome prediction in critically ill patients.

detail.abstract: Quantum entanglement is a phenomenon in which two physical systems are correlated in such a way that they appear to instantaneously affect one another, regardless of the distance between them. As commonly understood, Bell's Theorem famously demonstrates that any causal explanation of entanglement must discard either locality (the principle that nothing, including information, travels faster than light) or classical notions of realism (or both). Drawing on this concept, several legal scholars have metaphorically described 'entangled' legal concepts. For instance, if a state's highest court redefines the concept of 'foreseeability' in negligence law, this redefinition alters the concept of 'reasonable care' immediately in the eyes of the law. Godfrey (2024) is the first work to mathematically model entangled legal concepts, particularly in the context of legal interpretation. Here, we extend the quantification to the formulation and delineation of law (lawmaking) and the adjudication of law (judgment). In so doing, we connect legal entanglement to Sichelman's (2022) work on legal entropy, complexity, and the informational content of law. In addition to quantifying entanglement across various legal contexts, our approach provides broader insights. For example, it offers a more comprehensive analysis of the uses and limits of 'modularity' in law--specifically, the role legal boundaries (spatial or intangible) play in reducing information costs within legal systems. Moreover, we discuss how our model can improve theories of legal artificial intelligence. Finally, we explore the application of legal theory back to physics. If quantum physical entanglement operates analogously to legal entanglement, it requires discarding both locality and classical realism, though not in the manner commonly imagined.

detail.abstract: What information in earnings conference calls do investors respond to? We address this question by linking analyst forecast revisions to the textual content of earnings calls. An initial sentiment analysis shows that both analysts and stock prices tend to underreact to positive tones and overreact to negative tones. To further exploit the predictability of these biases, we augment numeric earnings variables with textual features from the earnings call and train a random forest model. Shapley values reveal that analysts react strongly to tangible information, such as verifiable operational facts, but respond weakly, or even incorrectly to vague or affective narratives. Translating predicted reaction bias into a trading signal, we construct a long-short portfolio that earns an annualized return of 17% with a Sharpe ratio of 1.27, unexplained by standard risk factors. The effects are more pronounced among firms with higher information uncertainty.

detail.abstract: Biodiversity loss and related regulations create material financial risks for firms relying on ecosystem services. We examine whether U.S. public firms adjust their financial flexibility in response to these exposures. Exposed firms improve financial flexibility, primarily by reducing long-term debt. These effects strengthen after the 2021 Kunming Declaration when biodiversity risk becomes salient, particularly among firms that perceive themselves as materially exposed. Responses are concentrated among firms with volatile cash flows, financial constraints, low climate exposure, and greater product-market competition, consistent with precautionary motives. Our results are robust across alternative biodiversity measures, highlighting how biodiversity risk fundamentally shapes corporate decision-making.

detail.abstract: BACKGROUND: The ability to replicate or manipulate spatial patterns is commonly used to detect cognitive impairments linked to neurological conditions like dementia and Alzheimer's disease, often through a constructional praxis test involving the copying of geometric shapes. While newer technologies like tablets provide digital alternatives for these tasks, older adults may find them difficult to use, leading to potential difficulties in participation or test performance. METHODS: Data from two waves of the Diagnostic Assessment of Dementia for the Longitudinal Aging Study in India (LASI-DAD) were used to compare the tablet version of a constructional praxis cognitive test with its traditional paper-and-pencil counterpart. Participants completed both versions of the test, with a 4.5-year interval between them, allowing us to examine differences in participation rates and performance between the tablet and paper-and-pencil formats. RESULTS: Considering the effects of demographic variables, cognitive decline, literacy and visual limitations, the results show that the test on the tablet caused no significant decrease in participation rate or accuracy in the drawings. Demographic factors such as age and literacy influence cognitive decline and test scores in our sample, as demonstrated by previous studies. CONCLUSION: Overall, the change to tablet-based administration of the test has slightly increased the participation and accuracy rate and has a positive effect on the assessment of the cognitive abilities of participants. The use of tablets does not appear to deter older participants. However, respondents with visual impairments tend to perform worse on the tablet version.

title: Which Market Leads Price Discovery? New Conclusions from a New Test

detail.title: Which Market Leads Price Discovery? New Conclusions from a New Test
detail.abstract: We show that the standard Granger causality test for assessing informational efficiency between financial markets is misspecified in the presence of market-microstructure noise, a pervasive feature of financial data. Although the test remains statistically valid, its economic interpretation is flawed: predictability from microstructure noise is misread as information flow. We propose a new test robust to such noise and apply it to credit markets, overturning established results. The corporate bond market, not the CDS market, leads in price discovery; there is no evidence of insider trading in CDS; and bond transactions contain more timely information than quotes.

title: The Citational Cartography of Power: A Post-Colonial Semiotics of the Indian Supreme Court

detail.title: The Citational Cartography of Power: A Post-Colonial Semiotics of the Indian Supreme Court
detail.abstract: This paper examines a fundamental tension in Indian constitutional practice: the Supreme Court’s continued reliance on Western legal frameworks despite India’s rich and distinct juridical heritage. Through detailed analysis of fifty landmark judgments delivered between 1950 and 2020, this study identifies a persistent "citational asymmetry"—a systematic judicial preference for Anglo-American jurists that marginalizes Indian legal thought, from classical dharmaśāstra to contemporary theorists. Drawing on post-colonial theory, I argue this practice constitutes a form of epistemic violence that silences indigenous conceptions of justice. In response, I propose semantic disobedience: a deliberate judicial methodology that integrates Indian legal philosophy into mainstream jurisprudence. This approach seeks not to reject Western influence altogether but to establish a more balanced, authentically Indian constitutional discourse that reflects the nation’s unique legal identity and intellectual traditions.

detail.title: An Agent-Based Model of Monetary Policy Transmission in an Emerging Economy: Comparing Quota and Corridor Systems in Nepal's Interbank Market
detail.abstract: An agent-based model (ABM) of the interbank market is simulated, aiming to test alternative monetary policy frameworks in the context of Nepal. The model is designed based on Bertrand Competition and Nash Bargaining Theory in a perfect information system with variables of liquidity assessment and risk pricing. Two distinct policy regimes are compared: a novel quota-based system, a hybrid price-quantity-based model, and the conventional corridor system. The findings indicate that the Quota model demonstrates superior efficacy in anchoring the interbank rate towards the policy target with greater stability. However, it transfers the cost to the central bank.

title: Paper Castles, The Collapse of a Financial Empire

detail.title: Paper Castles, The Collapse of a Financial Empire
detail.abstract:
This paper investigates the systemic failures that culminated in the 2008 financial crisis, focusing on the interaction between deregulation, regulatory inaction, and misaligned risk incentives. Drawing on historical policy shifts, it traces how financial deregulation in the 1980s—beginning with the Garn–St. Germain Act and culminating in the repeal of Glass–Steagall—encouraged excessive leverage and speculative practices. The securitization boom, fueled by subprime mortgages and collateralized debt obligations (CDOs), was legitimized by rating agencies assigning inflated AAA ratings, while credit default swaps (CDS) magnified systemic vulnerability. Case studies of Lehman Brothers, AIG, and the Icelandic banking collapse demonstrate how mispriced risk and liquidity freezes triggered global contagion. The paper also highlights overlooked early indicators, such as durable goods order declines, which signaled internal economic stress before the collapse.

The findings argue that the crisis was not inevitable; regulatory bodies like the Federal Reserve and the SEC failed to exercise their oversight powers despite warning signals. Misinterpreting the crisis as a liquidity shortage rather than an insolvency event, the Federal Reserve deployed flawed interventions, including low-interest-rate bailouts, which worsened moral hazard. The analysis concludes by recommending stricter leverage controls, rating agency accountability, and real-time economic stress indicators to strengthen systemic resilience.

title: Navigating the Trade-Environment Nexus: Economic Growth, Trade Integration, FDI, Sectoral Composition, and Environmental Sustainability in ASEAN Economies With Robust Econometric Models

detail.title: Navigating the Trade-Environment Nexus: Economic Growth, Trade Integration, FDI, Sectoral Composition, and Environmental Sustainability in ASEAN Economies With Robust Econometric Models
detail.abstract: The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) represents a critical region for examining the interplay between economic growth, trade integration, and environmental sustainability, given its rapid industrialization and rising carbon dioxide (CO₂) emissions. This study investigates the determinants of CO₂ emissions in nine ASEAN economies (Brunei, Cambodia, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, and Vietnam) from 1991 to 2024 by focusing on economic growth, trade openness, sectoral composition, renewable energy consumption, population growth, and foreign direct investment (FDI). Employing advanced econometric techniques including Panel-Corrected Standard Errors (PCSE), Feasible Generalized Least Squares (FGLS), and System Generalized Method of Moments (System GMM) and the analysis addresses statistical challenges such as heteroskedasticity, autocorrelation and endogeneity. Results confirm that GDP growth and industrial activity significantly increase CO₂ emissions, reflecting scale effects, while renewable energy, services sector expansion, trade openness, and FDI mitigate emissions through technique and composition effects, supporting the pollution halo hypothesis. Population growth exhibits a counterintuitive negative effect potentially due to urban efficiencies. Forecasting models (Linear Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, and LSTM) indicate that Linear Regression and XGBoost provide superior predictive accuracy for CO₂ trends. These findings underscore the need for integrated policy frameworks to accelerate renewable energy adoption, embed sustainability in trade and investment policies and mitigate industrial emissions which is aligning with the ASEAN Plan of Action for Energy Cooperation (APAEC) 2021-2025 and the Paris Agreement. The study contributes to the environmental economics literature by addressing the heterogeneous impacts of trade and FDI, exploring non-linear dynamics, and leveraging advanced forecasting for policy-relevant insights.

detail.title: Trade Liberalization and Human Development: A Sustainable Development Agenda for South Asian Nations
detail.abstract: This study critically examines the nexus between trade liberalization and human development across South Asian nations within the South Asian framework, integrating macroeconomic, institutional and environmental dimensions. Drawing on panel data from 1990 to 2023 and employing dynamic econometric techniques including Arellano-Bond and IV-GMM estimators the analysis reveals that trade openness yields inconsistent impacts on the Human Development Index (HDI) contingent upon institutional quality, sectoral composition and ecological sustainability. While aggregate models suggest positive correlations between trade and HDI, fixed and dynamic specifications expose negative short-term effects highlighting structural vulnerabilities such as import-driven livelihood disruptions and fiscal leakage. Institutional robustness, particularly the rule of law, emerges as a critical long-term mediator while CO₂ emissions consistently erode development gains. These findings challenge classical trade theory's universalist claims and underscore the importance of inclusive governance, green industrialization and sector-sensitive trade strategies. By advancing a multidimensional framework grounded in Sen's capabilities approach this study contributes to rethinking development policy in South Asia, aligning trade integration with equitable and sustainable wellbeing.

detail.abstract:
This study investigates whether EU subsidiaries’ compliance with the Non-Financial Reporting Directive (NFRD), which was executed in 2018, generates spillover effects on the ESG performance of their non-EU parent companies. As sustainability disclosure regulations continue to proliferate globally, understanding their cross-border implications for corporate behavior is increasingly important.

Employing a difference-in-differences (DiD) method, this study compares the ESG performance between the U.S. MNCs with EU subsidiaries and those without from 2016 to 2020. In addition, this study also investigates the heterogeneity of spillover effects in the individual ESG domains. Three moderator variables are analyzed in the study, including the segment complexity, the extent of exposure, and the internal control weakness.

This study shows that U.S. MNCs with EU subsidiaries experience spillover effects of the NFRD mandate and have better ESG performance than those without, on average. The empirical findings also show that only one moderator variable, the internal control weakness, will influence the observed spillover effects.

By extending the spillover effects literature to the non-financial domain, this study demonstrates how sustainability regulations in one jurisdiction can indirectly shape corporate practices worldwide. The findings offer valuable insights for policymakers aiming to promote transparency and align global sustainability standards through disclosure-based interventions.

title: A Study of Tibetan Concepts of Purity and Waste Utilisation from an Ecological Anthropological Perspective

detail.title: A Study of Tibetan Concepts of Purity and Waste Utilisation from an Ecological Anthropological Perspective
detail.abstract: Existing studies mostly focus on waste management issues in modern societies, while offering little explanation regarding the disposal and utilization of waste within traditional societies. This paper adopts an ecological anthropological approach to examine how Tibetan notions of purity influence the disposal and reuse of waste. It finds that under the unique cultural background of Tibetan society and the ecological conditions of the Tibet Plateau, a rich and complex concept of purity has formed. This concept profoundly shapes local understandings and classifications of waste in daily life, constructing a long-standing system of resource reuse that plays an important role in promoting sustainable material utilization within the community. The Tibetan approach to waste disposal and reuse reveals an internal logic of ecological rationality that can be understood as a form of local environmental wisdom. It contributes positively to maintaining ecological balance and provides valuable insights for the modern management of rural household waste.

title: Clinical Utility Index in Pharmaceutical Decision-Making: A Review and Optimization of the Index Using Optimal Design Strategies via Particle Swarm Optimization
affiliations: Fudan University,  and University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA)

detail.title: Clinical Utility Index in Pharmaceutical Decision-Making: A Review and Optimization of the Index Using Optimal Design Strategies via Particle Swarm Optimization
detail.abstract: Background and Objective: Design strategies for identifying a dose that optimizes the Clinical Utility Index, which balances efficacy and toxicity, are rarely discussed. The objectives of this paper are to provide an overview of the Clinical Utility Index with examples and to introduce an effective numerical method for optimizing it for any statistical model. Methods: This paper reviews the Clinical Utility Index as a framework based on multi-attribute utility theory and its applications in pharmaceutical decision-making. Using the bivariate Emax model as an example, we propose particle swarm optimization, a state-of-the-art, nature-inspired metaheuristic algorithm, to identify the optimal dose. Results: This paper highlights the conceptual development of the Clinical Utility Index, its methodological advances, and its diverse applications. To facilitate the use of particle swarm optimization by practitioners, we developed an online tool that allows users to easily determine the optimal dose after entering the parameter values for their design problem. The tool also enables users to evaluate the robustness of the optimal dose under various model misspecifications. Because particle swarm optimization performs effectively without requiring strong technical assumptions, it can be applied to more complex models or alternative design criteria. Conclusions: The Clinical Utility Index provides a systematic and quantitative framework for evaluating tradeoffs among efficacy, safety, and other important attributes in drug development. This study is among the first to apply optimal design theory to the optimization of the Clinical Utility Index and to develop an innovative web-based tool powered by a general-purpose metaheuristic algorithm. The tool allows users to generate customized designs for the bivariate Emax model and examine their robustness. Related measures, such as desirability functions and the health utility index, can be similarly explored, offering future directions for methodological research.

detail.title: A Study on the Role of Data Governance in Enhancing Big Data Analytics Precision and Decision-Making in the Retail Industry
detail.abstract: The purpose of this quantitative study was to examine the relationship between data governance framework implementation and stakeholder perceptions, decision-making effectiveness, and big data analytics performance in the retail industry. Existing literature highlights the importance of structured governance for improving data management, yet few studies have empirically evaluated its influence on analytical and decision-making capabilities within the retail sector. A survey-based quantitative study with retail IT professionals found statistically significant associations between data governance implementation and each of the three outcomes. The findings suggest that the presence of formal data governance frameworks is associated with greater stakeholder recognition of their importance, enhanced decision-making, and improved big data analytics performance in the retail industry. This study contributes to the literature by empirically validating data governance as a strategic enabler and highlights future research directions, including the role of governance maturity, security considerations, and the integration of emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence and blockchain.

detail.abstract:
In an era of accelerated digital transformation, geopolitical turbulence, and organizational fluidity, social capital emerges not merely as a latent asset but as the foundation of organizational resilience. This paper introduces the Seven-Pillar Management Composite Strategy Theory (7P-MCST) — a meta-theoretical, practice-oriented framework that reconceptualizes social capital as a multi-modal, evolving ecosystem composed of seven interdependent pillars: Philosophical (PCST)¹, Network (SCNT)², Growth/Resilience (SGST)³, Adaptive Influence (CAIST)⁴, Consciousness/VDC (VDC)⁵, Three-Dimensional Social Capital Management (3D Model)⁷, and Global Integrated Strategy (GIST)⁶. 7P-MCST integrates ethical, cognitive, structural, cultural, digital, spiritual, and strategic dimensions into a single architecture for leadership, governance, and operational design.

Grounded in classical sociological scholarship (Bourdieu, Coleman, Putnam) and extended through contemporary strategic theories of networks and algorithmic governance, the model advances three central claims. First, durable organizational resilience requires ontological coherence (a philosophical seed) aligned with social-soil dynamics (networks, culture, trust). Second, the emergent interplay between human and algorithmic actors necessitates an explicit pillar for digital/algorithmic capital to secure algorithmic legitimacy and institutional trust. Third, leadership must function as strategic trusteeship—orchestrating meaning, moral integrity, and adaptive influence rather than exercising command and control.

This first phase (theoretical framing) presents: (1) a synthesized literature review tracing social capital from classical roots to digital networks; (2) the philosophical premises underpinning 7P-MCST; and (3) a conceptual map that positions the seven pillars within an integrated architecture for measurement and managerial action. The contribution is twofold: it offers a robust philosophical grounding for strategic social capital, and it lays the conceptual groundwork for operational tools (network analytics, narrative diagnostics, algorithmic legitimacy indices) to be detailed in subsequent phases.

title: Cisterns for Life: Climate Adaptation Policies For Water Provision and Rural Lives
affiliations: Federal University of Pernambuco, Bocconi University, Universidade Federal de Pernambuco, Getulio Vargas Foundation (FGV) - Sao Paulo School of Economics,  and Universidade Federal de Pernambuco

detail.title: Cisterns for Life: Climate Adaptation Policies For Water Provision and Rural Lives
detail.abstract: Billions of people worldwide travel long distances daily to fetch water that is often unsafe for human consumption. Climate change is expected to exacerbate this critical issue, which threatens the economic development of dry areas in addition to posing health risks. This paper evaluates a large-scale, low-cost climate adaptation program that built one million rain-fed water storage cisterns in Brazil's poorest and most drought-prone region. Using unique individual-level administrative data and a difference-indifferences design, we show that the program substantially improved economic and health outcomes, benefiting both adults and children in the household. Notably, within ten years, family dependency on cash transfers decreased by up to 34%, while formal job earnings increased by 20%. Hospitalizations associated with waterborne diseases fell by 16% among adults and 37% among children, and families' compliance with cash transfer conditionalities on child health and education improved. Additional evidence suggests that the economic gains were driven by a relaxation of time constraints: cisterns sharply reduced the time burden of water collection, allowing beneficiaries to dedicate more time to productive activities. A cost-benefit analysis indicates a high marginal value of public funds compared to a wide range of public policies.

title: Religious Diversity and Its Socio-Economic Consequences in Contemporary India
affiliations: Independent Researcher, Independent and Independent Research

detail.title: Religious Diversity and Its Socio-Economic Consequences in Contemporary India
detail.abstract: India is home to one of the most religiously diverse populations in the world, encompassing Hinduism, Islam, Christianity, Sikhism, Buddhism, Jainism, and numerous indigenous faiths. This diversity, while historically contributing to India's rich cultural fabric, also intersects with the country's complex socioeconomic landscape. The present study examines the socioeconomic consequences of religious diversity in contemporary India, focusing on how religious affiliation correlates with income distribution, educational attainment, employment, and social mobility. Drawing on data from the Indian Census (2011), the National Sample Survey (NSS), and secondary literature, this study employs a mixed-methods approach combining statistical analysis with qualitative insights. The findings reveal that religious diversity in India has a dual character: it fosters social pluralism and intercultural exchange but also coincides with enduring economic inequalities. Certain minority communitiesparticularly Muslims and Dalit Christians-continue to experience socioeconomic marginalization manifested in lower literacy rates, limited access to formal employment, and higher poverty incidence. Conversely, regions with higher levels of interreligious coexistence tend to demonstrate stronger social cohesion and higher development indicators. The study concludes that religious diversity in India is neither inherently divisive nor uniformly beneficial. Its socioeconomic outcomes depend largely on institutional inclusion, equitable policy implementation, and intergroup relations. By analyzing the intersection of faith and socioeconomic structure, this research contributes to understanding how pluralism shapes development and social equity in a rapidly transforming society.

detail.abstract: Almost two years after Cyclone Idai hit Mozambique, Zimbabwe, and Malawi, thousands of people remain displaced. At the time, Idai was the most powerful cyclone to hit the Southern Hemisphere in two decades, but it is no longer an anomaly. Worse, the World Bank reports that climate change can potentially wipe out decades of social and economic progress in the developing world by displacing millions of people, many of whom will be pushed into poverty. Food and water insecurity connected to climate hazards-particularly in places dependent on agriculture-is a major factor that has forced families and whole communities to relocate for safety and subsistence. How do we solve the problem of climate-induced population displacement within the larger context of the global climate crisis? Across Africa, action on displacement is focused on rebuilding food security, water systems, and livelihoods decimated by the changing climate. detail.abstract: This paper investigates whether rainfall shocks affect the intra-household distribution of consumption in Malawi. Using four waves of household survey data and exploiting spatial-temporal rainfall variation across four agricultural growing seasons from 2010 to 2019, I estimate a resource allocation model to retrieve consumption shares for men, women, and children. The findings show that droughts tend to shift household resources from women and children to men. Welfare analyses indicate that women are more likely to bear the brunt of these shocks. This redistribution is likely linked to existing gender gaps in access to off-farm employment, which restrict women's ability to contribute to household income when their farming activities are disrupted by droughts. In contrast, men's relatively better access to off-farm work strengthens their role as the primary breadwinner, giving them greater access to household resources.

title: Macroeconomic Reports and the Cross-section of Industry Returns

detail.title: Macroeconomic Reports and the Cross-section of Industry Returns
detail.abstract: We show that the textual content of macroeconomic reports from the Federal Reserve and OECD predicts the cross-section of industry returns. Using a two-stage framework that combines large language models with classical machine learning to mitigate look-ahead bias, we extract textual signals that forecast six-month industry returns out-of-sample. An equal-weighted long-short portfolio sorted on these signals earns a six-factor alpha of 91 basis points per month. The effect is weaker for value-weighted portfolios and decays over time, consistent with slow information diffusion and arbitrage frictions. Our textual factor provides incremental information beyond standard macroeconomic variables and is robust across model specifications and time periods. Our findings suggest that complex, qualitative information in public reports is costly to process and is incorporated into asset prices only gradually.

detail.abstract: We propose money-metric asset valuation as a new hybrid valuation method that measures 'an investor's asset valuations' by combining and improving upon market valuation of assets and hedonic valuation of assets in many respects. Money-metric asset values represent an investor's preference over assets and they relate simply and meaningfully to the riskiness of assets, the investor's attitude to risk, expected arbitrage-free market values of assets, and hedonically optimal asset portfolios.

detail.abstract: Almost two years after Cyclone Idai hit Mozambique, Zimbabwe, and Malawi, thousands of people remain displaced. At the time, Idai was the most powerful cyclone to hit the Southern Hemisphere in two decades, but it is no longer an anomaly. Worse, the World Bank reports that climate change can potentially wipe out decades of social and economic progress in the developing world by displacing millions of people, many of whom will be pushed into poverty. Food and water insecurity connected to climate hazards-particularly in places dependent on agriculture-is a major factor that has forced families and whole communities to relocate for safety and subsistence. How do we solve the problem of climate-induced population displacement within the larger context of the global climate crisis? Across Africa, action on displacement is focused on rebuilding food security, water systems, and livelihoods decimated by the changing climate. Efforts have also sought to bolster ecological systems in response to environmental changes that occur over time (like desertification and sea-level rise) and which threaten the continent.

title: Characterisations of Efficient Social Outcomes
affiliations: Delhi School of Economics, University of Delhi

detail.title: Characterisations of Efficient Social Outcomes
detail.abstract: We consider a number of general versions of the planner's problem of choosing a social outcome. The versions differ in terms of the notion of social welfare that is used, the nature of admissible beliefs about the unknown state, whether the planner chooses outcomes deterministically or randomly, and whether the planner's future choices can be conditioned on the state to be revealed in the future. For planner's problems defined by various combinations of these features, we characterise the efficiency of a choice with respect to the given problem in terms of its optimality, leading to dualities between the two notions. The resulting identification of the complete set of efficient choice for a particular problem is useful when efficiency is considered necessary for a desirable choice but other criteria are to be used subsequently to make a final decision.

title: The Effect of Social Trust on Economic Growth with Emphasis on the Case of Iran

detail.title: The Effect of Social Trust on Economic Growth with Emphasis on the Case of Iran
detail.abstract: Today, most social and economic scientists have accepted the important role of extra-economic factors such as social trust in the process of economic development of societies. According to them, public trust is not only effective by creating cooperation and coordination between individuals and groups and reducing the costs of production, distribution and exchange in the economic system, but also in many other ways on economic growth. This article, while examining the ways of influencing social trust on economic development, tries to provide a conceptual framework and a practical definition of social trust and its adaptation to the conditions of growth in today's Iranian society. In this research, the method of applying the model of social trust to the last four decades of Iranian society and several approaches have been used for the model of the mechanism of the effect of social trust on economic growth. The article concludes: "Responsibility, efficient management, increasing business transactions, reducing possible risks in transactions, increasing domestic and foreign investment, reducing investment costs, creating welfare states" among the factors. They are an effective mediator in the mechanism of social trust and economic growth.

The associated long-run diversification potential of these markets is found to be much smaller than previously established. This is confirmed with a series of portfolio allocation exercises that reveal stark differences between short-and long-run allocation weights.

detail.abstract: We study how to communicate climate policy in economies dependent on fossil fuels by replicating the survey experiment of Dechezleprêtre et al. (2025) in Russia and extending it to include presidential-decree messaging and trust measurement in communicators. Russians' climate beliefs and knowledge broadly mirror citizens in other countries, though skepticism is slightly higher on core items in fossil-fuel dependent regions. Physics-based educational videos increase factual understanding, while videos focusing on economic measures to take action decrease support for climate policies-consistent with cost salience and low trust in economists. By contrast, cues from a political authority raise support for policy action.

title: Tax-Motivated Firm Splitting

detail.title: Tax-Motivated Firm Splitting

detail.abstract: How do corporate tax systems shape the boundaries of the firm? This paper shows that nonlinear corporate income taxation can distort firms' organizational structures by inducing tax-motivated firm splitting. I use administrative data on corporations and their owners and exploit two reforms that altered the tax benefits and costs of dividing a firm into multiple entities. First, I show that a temporary increase in the tax advantage of splitting reduces the share of firms filing jointly for corporate income tax purposes. Second, once the benefit is perceived as permanent and minimum capital requirements for new firms are abolished, the number of firms per entrepreneur rises significantly and persistently. Finally, I show that reorganizations are primarily driven by tax motives, as I find no effect on firms' total assets, employment, or industry diversification. These findings highlight extensive-margin responses of business organization to corporate taxation, with relevant implications for the understanding of firm dynamics and for tax design.

title: International Remittances and Intra-Household Risk-Sharing
affiliations: University of Nebraska at Omaha

detail.title: International Remittances and Intra-Household Risk-Sharing
detail.abstract: A large body of research has established the empirical and quantitative importance of international remittances as an insurance mechanism against income shocks in developing countries. However, households have additional self-insurance mechanisms, including precautionary savings, labor supply adjustments, and multiple earners. This paper develops a model with heterogeneous two-member households and endogenous international remittances to study the relationship between remittances from overseas workers and other self-insurance mechanisms. I calibrate the model with data from the Dominican Republic, and then use the model to decompose the relative importance of the self-insurance mechanisms used by non-migrant households and households with overseas workers. I find that the response of household behavior (remittances, labor supply, and savings) differs greatly depending on whether the household is a migrant or non-migrant household and on whether the shock hits the overseas worker (usually male) or the left-behind family member (usually female). Allowing for correlated wage shocks within non-migrant households further highlights the insurance benefits of migration by reducing joint exposure to local shocks and altering the composition of self-insurance mechanisms.

title: Determinants and Forecasting of Corporate Greenwashing Behavior
affiliations: , University of Regensburg - Department of Finance, University of Augsburg and University Augsburg

detail.title: Determinants and Forecasting of Corporate Greenwashing Behavior
detail.abstract: This paper empirically analyzes the determinants of corporate greenwashing behavior to enhance the forecasting and mitigation of greenwashing practices, particularly in the context of stakeholder decision-making. Using company-level characteristics of a sample of STOXX Europe 600 constituents, we show that ESG and environmental (E) scores have a U-shaped relationship with greenwashing, indicating that greenwashing is more likely for companies with low and high (E)SG scores. Additionally, ESG disclosure score, company size, cash-to-assets, and capital intensity are positively correlated with greenwashing. Furthermore, greenwashing behavior is more prevalent in consumer-related industries than in other industries. After identifying the determinants of greenwashing, we investigate the forecasting of greenwashing behavior using machine learning models based on economic considerations. Overall, our analyses demonstrate how current and future greenwashing risk can be effectively assessed, enabling stakeholders such as investors and policymakers to better identify corporate greenwashing behavior and incorporate this risk into their decision-making.

title: Optimal Investment under Irreversible Consumption and Locally Risk-Seeking Preferences
affiliations: Chonnam National University, Kyung Hee University - Department of Applied Mathematics  and Ajou University

detail.title: Optimal Investment under Irreversible Consumption and Locally Risk-Seeking Preferences
detail.abstract: We study an infinite-horizon portfolio choice problem in which an investor cannot tolerate any decline in consumption. The agent also exhibits locally risk-seeking preferences of the Friedman-Savage type, creating alternating regions of risk aversion and risk loving. The interaction between the non-decreasing consumption constraint and local risk-seeking behavior generates an extreme form of habit formation and leads to a dynamic free-boundary structure. We transform the non-concave optimization problem into an equivalent concave one via the concave-hull technique and characterize the optimal consumption and portfolio policies in closed form. The investor optimally defers consumption adjustments despite sufficient wealth within the risk-seeking region, and a discrete jump in consumption occurs once a critical threshold is reached. The optimal portfolio displays trend-chasing behavior: higher risky exposure in booms and conservative allocation after upward adjustments. Numerical simulations show that the expected duration of the riskseeking regime increases with the agent's patience, the magnitude of the consumption jump, and the market risk premium. Finally, the model can also be interpreted in an actuarial context, where the non-decreasing consumption rule parallels ratcheted or guaranteed-increasing payouts in insurance and annuity products, offering a theoretical foundation for analyzing dynamic guarantee and bonus-adjustment mechanisms.

title: Testing Spillovers in Resource Conservation: Evidence from a Natural Field Experiment
affiliations: National University of Singapore (NUS) and Columbia University

detail.title: Testing Spillovers in Resource Conservation: Evidence from a Natural Field Experiment
detail.abstract: This paper studies the potential for behavioral interventions aimed at promoting resource conservation within one domain to induce spillovers in another. Through a large-scale natural field experiment involving around 2,000 residents, we assess the direct and spillover effects of real-time feedback and social comparisons on water and energy consumption. Three interventions were implemented: two targeting shower use and one targeting air-conditioning use. We document a significant reduction in shower use attributable to both water-saving interventions, but no direct effects on air-conditioning use from the energy-saving intervention. For spillovers, we precisely estimated null effects on air-conditioning use arising from the water-saving interventions, and vice versa.

detail.abstract: The study of maritime delimitation agreements has traditionally followed a “state-centric” approach, overlooking the human dimension affected by these agreements. Rising sea levels may alter baselines, potentially prompting renegotiation of existing maritime boundaries. This raises the question: which actors can participate in such negotiations? This research aims to rethink the state-centric focus of the Law of the Sea by exploring the potential participation of other international actors in the (re)negotiation of maritime delimitation agreements, similar to interventions seen in advisory opinions before international courts. The analysis focuses on three key actors: (i) coastal communities, (ii) indigenous peoples, and (iii) industries. It examines how these actors engage in such processes, starting from their established rights of access and participation in ocean governance, and evaluates how these rights are enshrined to ensure meaningful public participation in maritime boundary matters.

detail.abstract: We model how a central bank communicates its noisy forecasts (forward guidance) while taking into account its own uncertainty (confidence) and the public’s perception of the bank’s uncertainty (reputation for confidence). This creates a mismatch between the public and central bank’s interpretation of the bank announcement which induces the bank to communicate with partial transparency and deliberate imprecision. Moreover, with higher confidence (lower reputation) announcements are more precise. With text data from internal Fed documents and newspapers, we find communication patterns are largely consistent with the model except the Fed’s communication strategy underreacts to reputation compared to the model.

The central research question investigates how current governance frameworks and national policies contribute to the sustainable use of marine resources and the realization of Sustainable Development Goal 14 (SDG-14). Utilizing a multi-level analytical approach, the research assesses legal and policy frameworks at national, regional, and international levels, focusing on the application of IOR-approved norms and agreements. Special attention is given to India's O-SMART scheme, which emphasizes the country's commitment to advancing ocean research and supporting the Blue Economy through substantial investment and technological innovation. The study evaluates the effectiveness of these initiatives in enhancing ecological sustainability, economic potential, and societal well-being. The findings highlight the need for robust governance mechanisms and collaborative strategies to ensure the long-term health and productivity of ocean resources, thus contributing to sustainable development and environmental preservation in the Indian Ocean region.

detail.title: Labour Law And Economic Policy
detail.abstract: This book studies labour institutions from an economic perspective to justify their existence and the advantages that they bring to innovation, efficiency, productivity and economic growth. The philosophical foundations of labour law rely on the protection of the weaker party of the employment contract. However, after 40 years of political neoliberalism, these justifications seem insufficient for achieving progress in the area of labour and employment rights. This book changes the narrative of why we need labour standards. It begins with a study of the reasons that gave rise to labour law in the context of the Industrial Revolution and its evolution, and moves on to analyse the current context dominated by globalisation and economic digitisation. It then proceeds to study the main justifications for intervention in the labour market in the current business-economic context on a global scale: economic growth; predistribution of wealth; a meritocratic allocation of working conditions and equality among workers. Using case studies and examples from across the EU, the UK and the US, the book shows how the deregulation of labour markets harms innovation and the economy, especially when considering the challenges of platform work, algorithms and AI. It demonstrates that labour standards such as the minimum wage, sectoral collective bargaining and collective rights, protection against dismissal and discrimination, occupational risk prevention, and social security are necessary for the economy to function properly.
